cultivar: Urtica dioica (stinging nettle), leaf only; nettle root is a different product
processing: Young tops and leaves are cut in spring before flowering, dried in shade or warm air (which destroys the sting), stripped from the coarse stems and cut; no fermentation.
harvest_season: Spring, April to June, before the plants flower; a second cut of regrowth is taken after mowing in summer, but the spring leaf is finer.
appearance_dry: Dark green crumbled leaf with some thin stem pieces and a smell of hay.
appearance_liquor: Pale yellow-green turning to a greenish amber, clear.
appearance_wet: Soft dark-green leaf looking like cooked spinach.
taste_profile: Green, grassy and savoury, like the water from cooked spinach, with a soft mineral saltiness and a hay finish; mild and not bitter.

brewing.notes: Just-boiled water, 7–10 minutes; it does not go bitter and a longer steep gives a fuller, more savoury cup. A squeeze of lemon brightens it, and it blends well with mint or lemon balm, which most people prefer to nettle alone.

vintage_note: Sold year-round as cut dried leaf with a two-year best-before, from the previous spring's cut; fresh nettle is dark green and smells of hay, old nettle is olive-brown and smells of dust. It is sold as a pharmacy herb in much of Europe, often with the harvest year on the box, and by tea merchants as loose leaf or bags. Make sure the pack says leaf, since nettle root and nettle seed are separate products with different uses.
description:
Nettle is the weed that stings you on every path in Europe, and dried and steeped it makes a mild, green, savoury infusion that has been drunk as a spring tonic for as long as anyone can remember. It is as common in a British health-food shop as in a Ukrainian pharmacy or a German supermarket.

The young spring tops are cut before the plant flowers, which is when the leaf is tender and tastes best, and simply dried; drying destroys the sting. There is nothing else to it, so quality is about the season of the cut and the freshness of the leaf.

The cup is unlike most herbal teas: not floral, not fruity, but green and savoury, like spinach water with a faint mineral saltiness, and quite pleasant once you stop expecting sweetness. It needs a long steep, seven to ten minutes, and takes lemon well. Most people drink it blended, with mint, lemon balm or a little rooibos for body, and nettle is a classic quiet partner in 'detox' blends for exactly that reason.

Buy dark green leaf, not brown, from the latest spring harvest, and check that it is leaf rather than root. There is no vintage, no grades beyond the cut size, and nothing to fake.

It has traditionally been drunk as a cleansing spring tea and for its iron; whatever you make of that, it is cheap, caffeine-free and a useful base for your own blends, and fresh young nettle tops in spring make an even better, greener cup.
sources_note: origin_country is a judgement call; nettle tea is traditional across all of Europe.
history:
Nettles have been eaten for a very long time: people in Britain and Ireland made nettle stew in the Bronze Age, about 3,000 years ago, and in medieval Europe the young plant was also taken as a medicine. Several Native American peoples used it too.

The tea has no recorded starting point. Boiling water disarms the sting, so a soup or an infusion was always the easy way to consume the plant. Nettle soup is still a spring dish in Scandinavia, Finland, Iran, Ireland, the United Kingdom and Eastern Europe, and the tea belongs to the same habit of gathering the young growth.
